strengths: Novel and practically relevant reformulation of privacy-preserving video understanding: operating on frozen video foundation model latent features rather than raw pixels, avoiding costly retraining and enabling plug-and-play use with modern large VFMs (VideoMAE, V-JEPA, InternVideo).

First method to demonstrate privacy preservation across multiple heterogeneous downstream tasks (action recognition, temporal action detection, weakly-supervised anomaly detection) rather than being tailored to a single task, addressing a genuine limitation of prior pixel-level approaches (SPAct, TeD-SPAD).

Thoughtful loss design: clip-level self-supervised mutual-information-destroying objective, multi-task co-training, and a latent consistency loss specifically to prevent overfitting to seen proxy tasks and preserve generalization to unseen tasks -- supported by clear ablations (Tables 4, 5, 9).

Extensive experimental validation across five backbones of varying scale, multiple privacy/utility benchmarks, and thorough ablations (architecture choice, attention heads, training data scale, loss weighting), lending good empirical support to the core claims.

Practical efficiency benefits are well quantified: substantially fewer trainable parameters than baselines, faster training via precomputed frozen features, and favorable runtime-vs-performance curves (Fig. 4, Table 13).

Introduces new protocols to evaluate and partially mitigate gender presentation bias in action recognition, an underexplored area in video understanding, with results on both a controlled synthetic-bias benchmark (NTU) and a real-world imbalanced dataset (Toyota Smarthome).
weaknesses: Privacy evaluation is largely restricted to linear-probe attacks (VISPR cMAP, gait retrieval); there is no analysis against stronger/adaptive adversaries (e.g., nonlinear probes, adversaries aware of the AAM defense, or attempts to invert/reconstruct private attributes), which is important for validating true robustness of an anonymization method.

The core self-supervised privacy objective (minimizing similarity between static clip pairs to destroy shared spatial/private information) is conceptually a fairly direct extension of the mutual-information-based objective in Dave et al. (2022b)/Fioresi et al. (2023); the main technical novelty is the latent-space clip-level application plus the new consistency and multi-task losses, which is a reasonable but somewhat incremental algorithmic contribution.

Comparisons to prior pixel-level anonymization baselines (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, VITA) may be somewhat apples-to-oranges given the fundamentally different threat models (pixel vs. latent access), and the paper does not include other recent latent/feature-space privacy baselines if any exist, limiting the strength of the 'first' and 'outperforms' claims.

Gender bias evaluation uses a binary gender formulation (acknowledged by the authors as non-inclusive), and the bias mitigation appears to be a byproduct of the general privacy objective rather than an explicit, principled debiasing mechanism, so the generalizability of these bias results to other demographic attributes is unclear.

As explicitly acknowledged, the method cannot protect privacy if raw video must be transmitted/stored before feature extraction, which meaningfully restricts the real-world applicability of the framework to scenarios where feature extraction already happens on a trusted device.

Reported privacy leakage reduction percentages vary noticeably across backbones (e.g., 35.5% for I3D vs. ~29% for VideoMAE-B/VJEPA-H), and the headline '35%' figure in the abstract is not representative of results on the larger, more modern foundation models, which slightly overstates the generality of the main claim.

strengths: Introduces a practically motivated reformulation of privacy preservation for video foundation models: operating in latent space rather than pixel space avoids costly retraining of large pretrained utility models, which is a real limitation of prior pixel-level anonymization work (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, Wu et al.).

Broad empirical coverage across five distinct tasks (action recognition on three datasets, temporal action detection, anomaly detection) and across multiple backbones (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G), showing the method is not tailored to a single architecture.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies: AAM architecture choices (MLP vs self-attention, depth, head count), task-subset training to test generalization to unseen tasks, loss-component ablation, and training-set-scale analysis (data efficiency with HMDB51).

Lightweight adapter design offers a meaningful reduction in trainable parameters relative to full-model retraining baselines, which is relevant for practical deployment and even mentioned as useful for federated settings.

The proposed gender-bias evaluation protocols (NTU-Bias-F/M, Toyota Smarthome) are a useful methodological contribution to an under-studied area (human-attribute bias in video, as opposed to scene bias) and the paper shows the privacy objective has a secondary debiasing effect without explicit bias supervision.
weaknesses: Privacy evaluation relies almost entirely on a simple linear-probe attacker (cMAP on VISPR, gait retrieval) trained after anonymization; there is no adaptive/stronger-attacker evaluation (e.g., fine-tuned nonlinear attacker, attacker trained with knowledge of the AAM) to confirm that private information is genuinely destroyed rather than just linearly inseparable, which is a known weakness replicated from prior self-supervised privacy literature rather than addressed.

The latent consistency loss (heavily weighted at ωLC=100 by default) explicitly regularizes the anonymized features to stay close (L2) to the original features, which is in tension with genuine anonymization; the gait experiment (Table 6) shows that with this loss active, a sensitive temporal attribute (gait identity) is still fairly recoverable (53.45 vs 69.73 baseline), suggesting the method's generalization objective directly limits the depth of privacy protection for attributes correlated with retained temporal structure — an unresolved tension the paper acknowledges but does not solve.

The core technical contribution is somewhat incremental: the self-supervised mutual-information-destruction objective is directly adapted from Dave et al. (2022b)/Fioresi et al. (2023), now applied to clip-level latent features with an added consistency regularizer and multi-task co-training; the novelty is largely in problem reformulation and engineering rather than a fundamentally new technique.

Baseline comparisons are unbalanced: the only head-to-head comparisons with prior pixel-level methods (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, VITA, downsampling/blurring/blackening) use the smaller I3D backbone, while results on larger foundation models (VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, VideoMAEv2-G, InternVideo-H) are only self-compared against raw/unanonymized features, so the paper's central scalability claim is not benchmarked against any competing method at that scale.

The headline '35% reduction in privacy leakage' is inconsistent across backbones (35.5% for I3D down to ~28.9-29.0% for VideoMAE-B/VJEPA-H), and cMAP reductions of this magnitude are not clearly connected to real-world privacy risk (no human studies or reconstruction/inversion attacks demonstrating that sensitive content is actually unrecoverable).

The gender-bias analysis relies on a binary gender presentation label and an artificially injected spurious correlation protocol (NTU-Bias) whose generalizability to real-world, naturally occurring bias is only partially validated by a single additional dataset (Toyota Smarthome); the magnitude of bias-gap reduction is modest in absolute terms (e.g., 9.42%→5.44%, 5.75%→3.48%) despite being reported as large relative percentages.

No reported variance/multiple-seed results for the main utility/privacy tradeoff numbers or bias evaluation, making it hard to assess the statistical reliability of claimed improvements, several of which are within 1-2 points.

The project page link is empty and there is no explicit statement of code/model release, raising reproducibility concerns given the complexity of the multi-task training pipeline (multiple classifier heads, several loss weights, co-training schedule).

strengths: Novel and practically motivated problem formulation: moving privacy preservation from pixel-space to latent-feature space is well-justified given the common practice of storing/sharing extracted features from large frozen video foundation models, and addresses a real limitation (task-specificity and retraining cost) of prior pixel-level methods like SPAct and TeD-SPAD.

Broad and thorough empirical evaluation across five distinct tasks (action recognition on K400/UCF101/HMDB51, TAD on THUMOS14, anomaly detection on UCF-Crime) and five different video encoder backbones (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G), showing consistent trends and reasonable scalability claims.

Extensive and well-organized ablation studies (AAM architecture choices, loss component removal, task-subset training, latent-consistency weight, attention head count, training set scale) that support the design choices and give insight into why each component matters.

The paper introduces new, carefully constructed protocols for assessing perceived-gender bias in action recognition (NTU-Bias-F/M synthetic shortcut construction and the naturally imbalanced Toyota Smarthome evaluation), which is a useful side contribution connecting privacy preservation to fairness.

Computational efficiency argument is concrete and well-supported with parameter counts and wall-clock comparisons (Table 13, Figure 4), showing substantial reduction in trainable parameters and training time relative to prior pixel-level adversarial approaches.
Interesting analysis distinguishing static/spatial vs temporal private attributes (e.g., gait on Casia-B), showing the method's nuanced behavior under different loss configurations.
weaknesses: Privacy evaluation relies primarily on a single linear probe (cMAP on VISPR, similar linear classifiers elsewhere) as the 'attacker.' There is no evaluation against stronger/adaptive attackers (e.g., nonlinear probes, fine-tuned classifiers, or attackers that know the anonymization scheme), which weakens the strength of the privacy claims — a sufficiently motivated adversary might recover more private information than a simple linear probe suggests.

The core technical ingredients (contrastive/mutual-information-based privacy objective, adapter-style modules, consistency regularization, GAN-style adversarial training) are largely adapted from existing works (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, standard adapter/LoRA-like designs); the novelty is primarily in the combination and application to latent space and multi-task co-training rather than fundamentally new techniques.

Baselines in the main comparison table are almost all pixel-level methods (downsampling, blurring, blackening, VITA, SPAct, TeD-SPAD); more recent latent/feature-space or multi-task privacy methods mentioned in related work (e.g., STPrivacy, Peng et al. 2024) are not directly compared against, making it harder to judge SPLAVU's relative advantage over the most comparable recent alternatives.

No error bars, confidence intervals, or repeated-run statistics are reported for any of the main results or ablations, making it difficult to assess the statistical robustness of the reported improvements (e.g., the 35% privacy leakage reduction headline figure).

The method still requires training task-specific classifier heads for each downstream task (fTAR, fTT AD , fTAD), so claims of 'generalization to unseen tasks' are somewhat limited — it is generalization within the latent space to tasks not included in the co-training objective, but new task heads must still be trained/fine-tuned on the anonymized features, which is a less strong claim than full task-agnostic anonymization.

The acknowledged limitation that transmission of raw video prior to anonymization is unprotected is significant for many real-world deployment scenarios (e.g., edge devices, surveillance), yet this is only briefly mentioned rather than substantively addressed or discussed with respect to practical deployment pipelines.

Reproducibility is somewhat limited: the project page link is empty/placeholder, and there's no indication that code will be released, which matters for a method with many hyperparameters (several loss weights, architecture choices) that could be sensitive to tuning.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely useful reformulation of privacy-preserving video understanding by operating in the latent feature space of frozen video foundation models rather than at the pixel level, addressing a real practical limitation of prior task-specific, retraining-heavy approaches (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, Wu et al.).

The proposed AAM/SPLAVU framework is evaluated across a genuinely diverse set of downstream tasks (action recognition, temporal action detection, anomaly detection) and across multiple backbones of increasing scale (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G), showing consistent trends and demonstrating scalability to large modern VFMs with minimal trainable parameters.

Extensive and thoughtful ablation studies (loss components, AAM architecture, attention head counts, task-subset generalization, training-set scale, latent-consistency weight) that clearly justify design choices and support the generalization claims.

Additional analyses beyond the core method are valuable and rigorous: black-box/white-box inversion attack resistance, qualitative reconstruction analysis, gait recognition as a temporal-attribute stress test, video retrieval generalization, and a training-compute/parameter-efficiency comparison.

The proposed gender-bias evaluation protocols (NTU-Bias-F/M and Toyota Smarthome) are a novel and well-motivated contribution to an understudied problem in video understanding, and the method shows a meaningful, non-trivial byproduct benefit in bias mitigation without an explicit debiasing objective.
weaknesses: The headline '35% reduction in privacy leakage' figure is only achieved on the I3D backbone; for the larger and arguably more relevant modern backbones (VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H) the relative reduction is smaller (~29%) and absolute residual cMAP remains substantial (e.g., 49.92 and 51.42), suggesting privacy leakage is not fully mitigated at scale despite the abstract's framing.

Baseline comparisons against prior anonymization methods (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, Wu et al., downsampling/blurring/blackening) are only conducted on the older I3D backbone; there is no direct head-to-head comparison with these methods on the larger foundation-model backbones where SPLAVU's advantages are most emphasized, making the scaling claims partly asserted rather than directly benchmarked.

The framework is explicitly not robust to white-box inversion attacks, which the paper itself flags as an important unresolved limitation, leaving open questions about real-world deployment security when adversaries have model access.

The privacy evaluation relies primarily on a proxy classifier (cMAP via retrained attribute predictor), which, while standard in this literature, may not fully characterize residual leakage; stronger or more adaptive privacy attacks (beyond the inversion experiments) are not explored as thoroughly as they could be.

The gender-bias protocol explicitly relies on a binary gender formulation, acknowledged by the authors as not inclusive, limiting the generalizability of the bias-mitigation claims to more nuanced or diverse gender categorizations.

The method currently only supports global clip-level embedding tasks and explicitly cannot handle dense prediction tasks (segmentation, captioning, patch-wise embeddings), which somewhat narrows the claimed generality of 'video understanding' anonymization.

Some recent related privacy-preserving methods mentioned in related work (e.g., Peng et al. 2024) are not included as quantitative baselines, leaving the comparison set slightly dated relative to the field.

strengths: Addresses a genuine and under-explored limitation of prior pixel-level privacy methods: task-specificity and the need to retrain utility models, by moving anonymization into the latent space of frozen video foundation models.

Broad experimental coverage across multiple backbones (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G) and multiple downstream tasks (action recognition, TAD, anomaly detection), which is more comprehensive than prior single-task privacy works (SPAct, TeD-SPAD).
Extensive and fairly rigorous ablation studies (AAM architecture choices, attention head counts, loss weighting, task combination for generalization, training data scale) that support design choices.

Includes attack-resistance analysis (black-box and white-box feature inversion, reconstruction attacks) which is often missing from privacy-preservation papers and adds credibility to the empirical claims, even when results are mixed.
Proposes new protocols for evaluating perceived gender bias in action recognition (NTU-Bias, Toyota Smarthome), which is a reasonably novel addition connecting privacy preservation to fairness.
Demonstrates substantial reduction in trainable parameters and training time relative to baselines, supporting the practical/compute-efficiency motivation of the plug-and-play design.
weaknesses: The core privacy claim is only partially convincing: post-anonymization cMAP values remain fairly high in absolute terms (e.g., 41-54 across backbones, vs. baseline 63-76), not close to random-chance levels in most settings, suggesting meaningful residual private-attribute leakage rather than strong anonymization.

The method is not robust to white-box inversion attacks (Table 8), where cMAP recovers close to the raw-video baseline (73.7 vs 76.4). Since the AAM is explicitly motivated as a shareable, plug-and-play module, white-box access by an adversary is a realistic threat model, and this failure substantially undermines the paper's central privacy-preservation claim.

Privacy evaluation relies entirely on empirical adversarial classifiers (cMAP from trained attribute predictors) with no formal/theoretical privacy guarantee (e.g., information-theoretic bound or certified defense), leaving open whether the method generalizes to unseen or more sophisticated attackers beyond those tested.

The bias mitigation contribution feels somewhat tangential and under-analyzed; the paper shows an empirical correlation between the privacy objective and reduced subclass accuracy gaps but offers limited mechanistic explanation or theoretical grounding for why self-supervised privacy training should generalize to fairness.

Comparisons to prior anonymization baselines (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, VITA) are conducted only on the older I3D backbone, and more recent privacy-preserving baselines mentioned in related work (e.g., Peng et al. 2024) are not empirically compared, leaving the strength of the quantitative advantage somewhat unclear against current alternatives.

Despite being framed as 'plug-and-play' on a frozen encoder, the method still requires co-training several task-specific heads (TriDet, MGFN, AR classifier) jointly with the adapter, which is a less lightweight process than the framing suggests, and the utility/privacy trade-off is sensitive to hand-tuned loss weights (e.g., ωLC=100), suggesting some fragility in hyperparameter selection.
Evaluation datasets (Kinetics400, UCF101, HMDB51, THUMOS14, UCF-Crime) are relatively standard/dated; no evaluation on more recent, larger-scale or more diverse real-world video benchmarks.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated problem reframing: moving privacy preservation from pixel-level anonymization (which requires retraining task-specific utility models) to latent-space anonymization that is plug-and-play on frozen video foundation models, addressing a real practical gap as VFMs become standard for feature extraction and storage.

Extensive and diverse empirical evaluation spanning five task families (action recognition, temporal action detection, weakly-supervised anomaly detection, private attribute prediction, gait/temporal attribute recognition) across many datasets (Kinetics400, UCF101, HMDB51, THUMOS14, UCF-Crime, VISPR, VP-HMDB51/UCF101, Casia-B, NTU, Toyota Smarthome).

Strong generalization/scalability demonstration across multiple backbones of increasing scale (I3D, VideoMAE-B, VJEPA-H, InternVideo-H, VideoMAEv2-G), with consistent privacy gains and minimal utility loss.

Thorough ablation studies (AAM architecture choice, attention head count, loss component contributions, task-subset training, latent consistency weighting, training data scale) that convincingly justify design decisions and demonstrate generalization to unseen tasks.

Practical efficiency contribution: dramatically fewer trainable parameters (up to 88.7% reduction) and much faster training via precomputed frozen features, which is a meaningful advantage for real-world deployment and federated settings.

Inclusion of inversion-attack robustness experiments (black-box and white-box) and qualitative reconstruction analysis, which add credibility to privacy claims beyond simple classifier-based leakage metrics.

Introduction of new, carefully constructed protocols for assessing gender presentation bias in action recognition (NTU-Bias and Toyota Smarthome evaluations), extending the scope of the work beyond privacy into fairness, with empirical evidence that the privacy objective incidentally mitigates bias.
weaknesses: The core self-supervised privacy objective (mutual information reduction via contrastive/NT-Xent loss) is adapted fairly directly from prior pixel-level works (SPAct, TeD-SPAD); the main novelty lies in applying it in latent space with multi-task co-training and a consistency loss, which is a meaningful but somewhat incremental combination of known techniques.

Privacy evaluation relies primarily on classifier-based leakage metrics (cMAP via linear/MLP probes on a narrow VISPR1 attribute subset of 7 attributes), which may not fully capture real-world privacy risk from more sophisticated or adaptively trained adversaries; absolute post-anonymization cMAP values remain fairly high (40-55%), raising questions about practical adequacy of the privacy guarantee.

The method is explicitly not robust to white-box inversion attacks (where the attacker has access to fA), which is an important threat model for stored/shared features in many of the motivating scenarios (e.g., leaked model weights); this is acknowledged but not resolved.

No variance/error bars or multiple-seed results are reported for main tables, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the reported utility/privacy trade-offs, especially given some differences (e.g., 1-2% utility drops) are relatively small.

The framework is restricted to global clip-level embeddings/classification-style tasks; it explicitly cannot support dense prediction tasks (segmentation, captioning, detection with spatial outputs), limiting the claim of general applicability to 'video understanding' broadly.

Gender bias evaluation is limited to a binary male/female formulation (acknowledged by the authors as a limitation), and the artificial bias injection protocol (NTU-Bias) using single spurious correlation per split is a somewhat narrow proxy for real-world bias phenomena.

Comparisons to prior anonymization methods (SPAct, TeD-SPAD, VITA) are conducted primarily on an older I3D backbone where those methods were originally designed, while the proposed method's large-backbone experiments lack equivalent baseline comparisons, making some advantage claims partly based on different operating points rather than apples-to-apples comparisons.
